reviewBoundary: Four complete junior insertion originals in two practices. Diary and guide-specific heading/quotation/candidate structure retained. Same-author all-placement review, fictional cases, not independent calibration.

units.title: Two diaries: a ferry and a rehearsal
units.alignmentNote: Two complete four-gap/five-option diary passages. Each candidate at most once; one unused sentence in each.

materials.title: An earlier boat
materials.instruction: Read the whole diary. Use each option at most once. One sentence is not needed.
materials.text:
Sunday, 9 March

We planned to take the ferry across the river today. Dad had checked the sailing times on Friday, but Mum asked us to look again before leaving. ____1____ The notice explained that work at the landing place had changed the afternoon service.

Our planned boat would leave thirty minutes earlier. We could still catch it if we left home at once, but my brother had not finished packing his bag. ____2____ He chose the one thing he wanted for the short journey, rather than bringing his whole toy box.

At the landing place, a staff member showed us which queue to join. A second queue was for a boat going farther along the river. ____3____ The people in front of us were travelling to a village we had never visited.

Our crossing lasted only fifteen minutes. I stood with Dad where the staff said it was safe to watch the water. On the other bank, we bought lunch and planned our walk. ____4____ This time, the timetable we used was the new one.
candidates: A. We checked the return journey before walking away.
B. The first page we opened contained an update.
C. He put his small red car into the bag and closed it.
D. We asked about the destination before following them.
E. The afternoon service had never changed in any way.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B introduces the update explained by the next sentence. C packs, D checks a queue and A return timing fit later gaps; E contradicts the notice.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: C completes the brother’s packing and supplies the one toy mentioned next. A/B/D concern timetables/queues; E denies the real change.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: D checks the queue’s destination, preparing the different village. A/B concern service timing and C the bag. E contradicts the update rather than avoiding a wrong boat.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: A connects arrival with a return check, and this time refers to using the new timetable. B was initial discovery, C packing and D outbound queue. E is false.

materials.title: Listening from the back row
materials.instruction: Read the whole diary. Use each option at most once. One sentence is not needed.
materials.text:
Thursday, 13 March

Today our music group rehearsed in the hall instead of the classroom. I usually played beside the piano, where I could hear every note clearly. ____1____ From there, the balance sounded different.

Our teacher asked another student to play my part while I listened. The piano was much louder than I had realised, and the quiet opening of the recorder tune was difficult to hear. ____2____ We tried it again, this time with the pianist playing more softly.

The change helped, but I still missed the first note. I had been looking down at the music when the group began. ____3____ Once I could see the starting signal, I came in with the others.

At the end, we returned the chairs to their normal places. I wrote two reminders at the top of my page: listen across the room, and watch the start. ____4____ It was a better result than simply playing the same passage louder.
candidates: A. The teacher moved my stand slightly so I could see her hand.
B. I had learned something about both sound and timing.
C. She sent me to listen from the back row first.
D. I described the missing recorder sound to the group.
E. The only solution was for every instrument to play as loudly as possible.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: C establishes the new listening position picked up by From there. D reports balance, A improves sight and B sums up later learning; E conflicts with the softer-piano test.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: D reports the observed recorder problem and motivates softer piano. C is position, A view and B final learning. E would worsen balance.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A creates a view of the teacher’s hand, referred to by starting signal. C/D concern hearing and B summary; E does not fix seeing the cue.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: B summarises sound and timing, the two written reminders. A/C/D are earlier actions; E contradicts the final rejection of merely louder playing.

units.title: Two guides: finding a route and making a request
units.alignmentNote: Two complete five-gap/seven-option guides. Three headings remain printed; gap2 is inside quotation marks and gap5 is a heading. Two unused candidates in each; do not import an extra once-only rule.

materials.title: Planning a walk in a new town
materials.instruction: Read the whole guide. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.
materials.text:
Finding a route in a new town begins with knowing where you want to arrive. A place name alone may be unclear if several buildings use it. ____1____ That small check can prevent a confident walk to the wrong branch of a museum or library.

Ask a precise question

When asking for help, give a useful starting point. You might say, "____2____" A person can answer more easily when they know both your destination and your current position.

Choose a suitable route

The shortest line on a map may include steps or a steep hill. ____3____ A slightly longer walk may fit your group better than the route suggested first.

Keep the information current

Roadwork or a closed gate can change a familiar path. ____4____ If a sign at the site disagrees with an old saved route, pause and check rather than forcing your way through.

____5____

Before leaving the destination, consider how you will get back. The return route may look different after dark, and public transport may run less often later. Keep enough time and an appropriate plan for the whole outing.
candidates: A. Check whether the directions reflect recent local changes.
B. Is this the way from the station to the museum on King Street?
C. Include the journey back
D. Confirm the full address and the entrance you need.
E. A closed gate is permission to climb over it.
F. Consider distance, access and the needs of the people walking.
G. The shortest route must be suitable for every person.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: D specifies address/entrance and explains avoiding the wrong branch. B quoted question, F route suitability, A updates and C return heading fit later gaps. E/G impose unsafe or universal assumptions.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: B is a first-person location-to-destination question suited to the surrounding quote. A/D/F are general directions and C a heading. E/G do not ask for help.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: F checks needs/access beyond shortest distance, preparing a longer suitable route. A/B/C/D concern other stages. G denies varied access needs; E ignores closure.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: A asks for current information, illustrated by roadwork/signs. B/C/D/F concern questions, return, address and suitability. E/G contradict caution or varied needs.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: C heads the return-planning paragraph. A/B/D/F address outward information, while E/G do not concern a safe whole outing.

materials.title: Asking someone to change a plan
materials.instruction: Read the whole guide. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.
materials.text:
Sometimes a shared plan no longer works for you. Asking for a change can be easier when you explain the specific problem rather than suggesting that everyone else has been inconsiderate. ____1____ This helps separate the difficulty from a judgment about the other people.

Make the request specific

A vague complaint can leave others unsure what you want. You might say, "____2____" A clear alternative gives them something concrete to consider.

Listen to the reply

Others may have limits you did not know about. ____3____ A question about their situation can reveal another way to solve the problem without demanding your first choice.

Agree on what changes

If the group finds an alternative, make sure everyone understands the new arrangement. ____4____ Otherwise, one person may follow the old plan while another follows the new one.

____5____

Afterwards, notice whether the change solved the original difficulty. Thank people for helping, and mention any remaining problem while it is still specific. An arrangement can be revised without treating the whole relationship as a failure.
candidates: A. Could we meet at four instead, so I can come after my appointment?
B. They must accept your suggestion even if it creates a new difficulty.
C. Review how it worked
D. Describe which part of the arrangement has become difficult for you.
E. Repeat the agreed time, place or responsibility before ending the discussion.
F. Their first answer may therefore be different from the one you hoped for.
G. A changed plan means that nobody can ever be trusted again.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: D identifies a specific difficulty, picked up by This, rather than blame. A quote, F other limits, E confirmation and C review serve later gaps. B/G impose unreasonable demands or judgments.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: A is the specific quoted alternative with a reason. D/E/F are general descriptions and C a heading. B/G do not request a workable change.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: F follows from hidden limits and leads to asking about their situation. A/D/E concern request/problem/agreement; C final review. B ignores their limits.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: E repeats the agreed details, preventing old/new confusion. A initial request, D problem, F response and C review belong elsewhere. B/G do not confirm the arrangement.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: C heads checking whether the change helped. A/D/E/F concern earlier stages. B/G reject mutual adjustment rather than evaluate it.
